Not sure. It looks like a hand clamping electrode with copper tips. Probably a specialty tool or home made. I'm guessing he's using a welder with a foot pedal. He must cut the power before he releases the metal piece via foot pedal, otherwise you would see an arc flash upon release. Very interesting stuff, smart thinking. The dent doesn't look brand new, like off the factory line new, but it's a good repair job.

I wondered why he didn't electrocute himself or burn himself. There's enough current there to melt metal, so you think it would be dangerous. He wasn't wearing gloves either. And how did he get the little tabs off? They were welded strongly enough to be able to pull the frame into shape without coming off.

Welding is dangerous, it uses live electricity to weld two pieces of metal together usually with a filler rod to add the puddle being welded.

There are many different types of welding, Shield Metal Arc Welding, (SMAW) Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW), Tugsten Inert Gas (TIG). These however run on the same principle of electricity. A welding machine, basically controls voltage and amperage in a circuit. This machine has two electrical conductors run through thick copper wires. On one end is a clamp (usually positive +), this clamps to the work, in this case, the frame that has the dent. The other end (usually negative -) holds a filler rod (stick), or is a gun that feeds wire to the melting pieces.

In this case, the negative electrode holds the tab that is going to be welded. The positive electrode is probably clamped to the work somewhere close but out of sight in the video. Once the welding machine is turned on, it is 'live'. Meaning there is electricity present in terms of Voltage. There is no flow because the circuit is incomplete so there is no Amperage. Once you touch the two pieces together, the 'live' frame, and the tab complete a circuit of electricity. If enough Voltage is present you don't need to touch the pieces together, the electrical circuit will 'jump' from one electrode (the frame), to the other (the tab) if close enough. This is called an electrical arc. The arc causes extreme heat. So extreme that it melts metal.

The tabs he used have a ring on one end, for pulling purposes seen here, and then have a thick metal bit, for strength, and comes down to a small pointed tip. The tip is small so that it will melt first to the frame, it melts to a small point.

So to review, the frame is clamped with a positive electrode, the tab is a negative electrode. The welder is turned on. The frame is live, has electricity ready to flow through it, the man touches the tab to the frame, it arcs, creating heat and melting the tab to the frame, he turns the welder off and releases the tab. He does this many times, and then runs a rod through the rings, and then uses a hydraulic tool to pull all the tabs together and take the dent out.

He got the tabs off by twisting and bending the welds. For example, take a piece of wire from an alarm clock or something and try to pull the wires so it fails. It's very difficult. But if you bend it back and forth and twist it, it should break easy.
